summary: Defines procedures for specifying and registering media types for use in MIME and other Internet protocols. It is a Best Current Practice and was later replaced by RFC 6838.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared list of file type labels needs rules for adding new labels. This memo is that rulebook.

questions: how to register a media type
what is the vendor tree vnd
subtitle: The rules for naming, describing and registering media types such as text/plain with IANA.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as MIME can carry arbitrary labeled content, so the labels need an orderly, well-specified and public registration process.
tldr.mechanism: Media types are registered with IANA in trees (standards, vendor, personal) that have different requirements, using a common naming syntax, a registration template and a review by a media types reviewer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4288 replaced RFC 2048 and moved the process out of the MIME document set. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 6838.

today: RFC 4288 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 13) that is now obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 6838. It had itself replaced RFC 2048.

sections.title: Why Media Types Need Registration
sections.content:
Many protocols, including MIME, can carry arbitrary labeled content. A mechanism is needed to label it, and a registration process for the labels, so that the set of values develops in an orderly, well-specified and public manner. This document uses the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as a central registry.

The process began for Internet mail, where limiting the number of types helped interoperability. That proved too restrictive for other environments. It was generalized in RFC 2048, and this document moves it out of the MIME set to show it is independent of MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone could invent file labels with no list, nobody would agree on what they meant. A shared list keeps things tidy.

sections.title: Registration Trees and Names
sections.content:
Subtype names can be grouped into registration trees, each with its own requirements.

  • Standards tree: for types of general interest. Registrations MUST be approved by the IESG and MUST correspond to a formal publication by a recognized standards body. Names are normally not faceted (no period).
  • Vendor tree: for types tied to commercially available products, with the leading facet vnd.. Anyone may submit, but the registration belongs to the vendor, and it may go directly to IANA.
  • Personal or vanity tree: for experimental or non-commercial types, with the leading facet prs..
  • Special x. tree: unregistered, experimental names. Types here MUST NOT be registered, and both x- and x. forms are discouraged.

IANA may, with IESG consent, create additional top-level trees, announced through an IESG-approved RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different shelves: one for official standards, one for company products, one for personal projects, and one for unofficial experiments that are never listed.

sections.title: What a Registration Must Satisfy
sections.content:
A media type MUST function as an actual media format. Things better described as a transfer encoding or a charset cannot be registered, so base64 cannot be a media type. Every type has a type name and a subtype name, both case-insensitive, of 1 to 127 characters drawn from letters, digits and ! # $ & . + - ^ _. Names beginning with X- MUST NOT be registered, and subtypes that are not XML MUST NOT end in +xml.

The top-level types discussed are text, image, audio, video, application, multipart and message. A new top-level type MUST be defined by a standards-track RFC.

Each type MUST use a single canonical data format. Standards-tree types need parameters fully specified and a precise, openly available format specification. Vendor-tree specifications may not be public, while personal-tree specifications may be published as RFCs or deposited with IANA. Universal support of a type is not required, but a type meant for limited use MUST say so.

The encoding considerations field takes the values 7bit, 8bit, binary or framed.
sections.plainLanguage: A label has to describe a real kind of file, be spelled with allowed characters, and come with a clear description of the format.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure is an administrative one, not a formal standards process. For the standards tree, notice MUST be sent to the ietf-types mailing list for review and the IESG MUST approve before registration. Vendor and personal registrations go directly to IANA, ideally after posting to the list.

IANA passes registrations to a media types reviewer appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director(s). Registrations that do not meet the requirements are returned for revision, and the reviewer's decisions may be appealed to the IESG. Otherwise IANA registers the type and makes it available. Registrations are listed at the IANA media-types page.

Vendor and personal types are registered automatically if minimal conditions are met: a real media format, well-formed unique names with the right tree prefix, a format specification (or pointer) for personal types, and a reasonable security considerations section.
sections.plainLanguage: You fill in a form, people can comment, a reviewer checks it against the rules, and if it passes the label goes on the official list.

sections.title: Changes, Comments and the Template
sections.content:
The owner of a type may request changes, which follow the same procedure as the original registration. Changes should be requested only for serious omissions or errors, and may be denied if they would make previously valid entities invalid. Owners can pass responsibility to someone else, and the IESG can reassign it. Registrations may not be deleted. A type no longer believed appropriate is marked OBSOLETE in its intended use field.

Community members can send comments on registered types to IANA, which are reviewed and passed to the owner and may be attached to the registration. The registration template has fields such as type name, subtype name, parameters, encoding considerations, security considerations, interoperability considerations, published specification, intended usage (COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE), and change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a label is listed it can be fixed by its owner, but it is never erased. Old labels are just marked OBSOLETE.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
This document's own security section points to section 4.6. An analysis of security issues MUST be done for standards-tree types, and is encouraged for vendor and personal types. Whatever analysis is done, descriptions MUST be accurate, and all known security risks MUST be identified. Saying there are no security issues must not be confused with the issues not having been assessed.

Issues to consider include active content that can act on the recipient's files, directives that disclose information, compression that can expand enormously to consume the recipient's resources, and types that need external security services they do not provide themselves. Registrations MUST state whether they use active content and what steps protect users.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone adding a file label must honestly say what could go wrong with it, such as files that run programs or unpack into something huge.
